text:
Sampled ranking can change both metric values and model ordering; performance against 99 negatives is not a reliable proxy for full-catalog retrieval. RecSys 2025’s [sampling-reliability study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) distinguishes resolution, fidelity to full evaluation, robustness, and recovery of model rankings. A [2024 sequential-recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) found that aggregate results conceal head/mid/tail differences: random negative sampling favored head items, while popularity-based methods offered more balanced performance with aggregate accuracy tradeoffs.

Suggested auxiliary audit, inferred from these findings: freeze training users and chronological prefix–next-item pairs within each category; these are training-fit diagnostics, not independent generalization estimates. Compare identical targets against fixed, unique candidates drawn uniformly, by training popularity, and by title/description TF-IDF similarity. Treat unobserved competitors as unlabeled, potentially relevant items. Compute exact full-catalog target ranks through chunked scoring, with consistent prefix-item masking and tie handling. Report HR@10, reciprocal rank, target-score margins against the strongest competitors, and results by training-frequency strata. Across checkpoints, compare sampled versus full-catalog model ordering and paired performance differences.

Repeat candidate draws with fixed seeds to quantify sampling sensitivity; bootstrap users within category for uncertainty, keeping each user’s prefixes together. Show category results and their macro-average; five users/category implies substantial uncertainty. Record candidate counts, distributions, masking rules, seeds, and runtime. These audits should remain separate from the unchanged host validation HR@10 used for selection. The [2024 rank-estimation paper](https://research.google/pubs/improved-estimation-of-ranks-for-learning-item-recommenders-with-negative-sampling/) supports caution about sampling-induced rank bias; it does not establish that harder candidate sets automatically estimate full-catalog performance better.
